column2: Grieving for Drona, their vigour struck down by stupor, those kings sat attending upon the son of Saradvat (Kripa).
Having comforted one another for a while with reasons in accord with the scriptures, at nightfall the rulers of the earth betook themselves to their own tents.
Above all, the son of the charioteer (Karna), King Suyodhana, Duhshasana and Shakuni found no sleep.
O descendant of Kuru, even in their dwellings those lords of the earth found no ease; brooding on the terrible destruction, they did not obtain sleep.
That night they gathered in Duryodhana's quarters, out of fierce hatred for the great-souled Pandavas.
Remembering how Krishna (Draupadi), tormented in the game of dice, had been dragged into the assembly, they burned with regret, their minds greatly distressed.
Thinking of the sufferings the sons of Pritha had been made to endure through the dice, O king, they passed that night with difficulty, as long as a hundred years.
Then, when the spotless dawn came, relying on the decree of fate, they all performed the necessary rites according to the prescribed rule.

Having made Karna their commander, with auspicious rites and festive ceremonies performed, and having had the best of the twice-born pronounce blessings with curd, vessels of ghee and unbroken rice grains,
with gifts of gold coins, cows, gold and costly garments, and cheered with benedictions of victory by the bards, panegyrists and minstrels,
so too the Pandavas, O king, having completed all their daily rites, came out of their camp resolved upon battle.
Then began the tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end, between the Kurus and the Pandavas, each bent on slaying the other.
For two days, O king, with Karna as commander, the fight between the armies of the Kurus and Pandavas was wondrous to behold.
Then, having wrought a very great slaughter of his foes in battle, Karna was struck down by Phalguna (Arjuna) before the eyes of Dhritarashtra's sons.
Thereupon Sanjaya went to the city named after the elephant (Hastinapura) and told Dhritarashtra all that had happened in the Kuru country.
[Janamejaya said:] The aged king, son of Ambika, who had fallen into the deepest grief on hearing that Bhishma and Drona had been slain in battle by the enemy,
how, O best of the twice-born, did he, in his sorrow, keep his life when he heard that Karna, who sought Duryodhana's good, was slain?
That king in whom he had placed the hope of his sons' victory, when he was slain, how did that scion of Kuru preserve his life?
Alas, I think it hard for men to die even in distress, since the king did not give up his life on hearing that Karna was slain.
And likewise hearing that his other friends, sons and grandsons had been felled, he did not abandon life; that, O Brahmana, I deem a hard thing.
O ascetic rich in penance, tell me all this in detail, for I am never satisfied with hearing the great deeds of my forefathers.
[Vaishampayana said:] When Karna was slain, O great king, Gavalgana's son (Sanjaya) that night, dejected, set out for Nagapura with horses swift as the wind.
Having reached Hastinapura with a mind greatly troubled, he went to the palace of Dhritarashtra, whose kinsmen had been destroyed.
Seeing the king, his vigour struck down by stupor, he joined his palms and bowed his head to the king's feet.
Having duly honoured Dhritarashtra, lord of the earth, and exclaimed "Alas, what misery!", he then spoke.

I am Sanjaya, O lord of the earth. Are you well? Having fallen into calamity through your own fault, I hope you are not bewildered today.
mahabharata:8:1.30	The wholesome counsels spoken by Vidura, Drona, Ganga's son (Bhishma) and Keshava you did not accept; I hope you do not now grieve, remembering them.
mahabharata:8:1.31	The good advice given in the assembly by Rama (Parashurama), Narada and Kanva was not heeded; I hope you do not grieve, remembering it.
mahabharata:8:1.32	Your friends, devoted to your welfare, led by Bhishma and Drona, have been slain by the enemy in battle; I hope you do not grieve, remembering them.
To him who spoke thus, the joined-palmed son of the charioteer, the king, afflicted with sorrow, sighing long, replied:

When the valiant son of Ganga, master of divine weapons, was slain, Sanjaya, and the mighty-bowed Drona, my mind was greatly pained.
mahabharata:8:1.35	That glorious one, born of the Vasus, who every day slew ten thousand armoured chariot-warriors,
mahabharata:8:1.36	was slain here by Shikhandin, son of Yajnasena, protected by the Pandavas; my mind is greatly pained.
mahabharata:8:1.37	He to whom Bhargava (Parashurama) gave the supreme weapon, he who in boyhood was taught archery by Rama himself,
mahabharata:8:1.38	by whose grace the mighty princes, sons of Kunti, and other lords of the earth attained the rank of maharatha,
mahabharata:8:1.39	hearing that Drona, truthful and mighty archer, had been slain in battle by Dhrishtadyumna, my mind is greatly pained.
mahabharata:8:1.40	Hearing that Drona, whose equal in the scriptures was not to be found among men in the three worlds, had been slain, what did my men do?
mahabharata:8:1.41	When the Samshaptakas had been routed by the great-souled Pandava Dhananjaya and sent by his prowess to Yama's abode,
mahabharata:8:1.42	and when the Narayana weapon of the wise son of Drona had been neutralised, what did my men do with the remnants of the shattered divisions?
mahabharata:8:1.43	I imagine them fleeing in disorder, plunged in an ocean of grief, with Drona slain, like boatless men drifting on the sea.
mahabharata:8:1.44	Duryodhana, Karna, Bhoja Kritavarman, Shalya the king of the Madras, Drona's son and Kripa,
mahabharata:8:1.45	and my remaining sons and the others, Sanjaya—when the divisions were scattered, what was the look on their faces?
mahabharata:8:1.46	Tell me all this truly as it happened, Gavalgani, in the battle, on both sides, the Pandavas' and mine.
[Sanjaya said:] O revered one, hearing what has befallen the Kauravas at the hands of the Pandavas, do not grieve; a mind set on what is desired is not pained.
For whether a thing is destined or not destined to befall a man, no wise person grieves at not obtaining it or at obtaining it.
[Dhritarashtra said:] There is no pain to me in hearing, Sanjaya; I consider this to have been ordained of old. Tell it as you wish.
All the weapon-bearers, O lord of men, stood with faces downcast, grief-stricken, not looking at one another and not speaking.
Seeing your troops in that distressed state, O Bharata, many in their grief and fear kept gazing upward.
O king, their weapons, all stained with blood, slipped from the tips of their hands when they saw Drona felled.
Those weapons, hanging loose and ill-omened, O great king, appeared like stars in the sky.
Seeing his own army thus afflicted, still and as if bereft of spirit, King Duryodhana spoke.

Relying on the might of your arms, I challenged the Pandavas to battle and began this war.
mahabharata:8:2.8	Now that Drona is slain it seems dejected, and warriors fighting in the battle are being killed on every side.
mahabharata:8:2.9	Victory or death comes to one who fights in battle; what is strange in that? Fight, facing every direction.
mahabharata:8:2.10	Behold the great-souled Karna, son of Vikartana, the mighty archer, moving in battle with divine weapons and great strength,
mahabharata:8:2.11	from whose terror in battle Dhananjaya, son of Kunti, always turns back in rage, like a small beast from a lion,
mahabharata:8:2.12	by whom mighty Bhimasena, possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants, was brought to that plight in a mere human fight,
mahabharata:8:2.13	by whom the heroic, illusion-working Ghatotkacha, versed in divine weapons, was slain in battle with the unfailing dart as he roared dreadfully.
mahabharata:8:2.14	Today in battle you shall see the inexhaustible wealth of arms of that wise, truthful warrior of unsurpassed prowess.
mahabharata:8:2.15	You shall witness the valour of Drona's son and of Radha's son, both great-souled, among the Pandava and Panchala hosts.
mahabharata:8:2.16	All of you are brave, wise, nobly born, virtuous and skilled in weapons; today you shall see one another's prowess.
When he had spoken thus, O great king, the mighty Karna, son of Vikartana, roared a lion's roar and fought on.
In the sight of all the Srinjayas, Panchalas, Kekayas and Videhas, he wrought great slaughter.
From his bow arrows issued in hundreds, clinging at head and feather like rows of bees.
Having afflicted the Panchalas and the mighty Pandavas, and having slain thousands of warriors, he was at last felled by Arjuna.
When that best of kings fell to the ground, overcome, a great cry of lamentation arose from the women, O best of the Bharatas.
That sound filled the whole earth; the women, O Bharata, sank in a most dreadful ocean of grief.
Approaching the king, Gandhari, O bull of the Bharatas, fell senseless to the ground, as did all the women of the inner apartments.
Then, O king, Sanjaya comforted those afflicted women, who were fainting again and again and shedding tears.
The comforted women trembled again and again, like plantain trees shaken on all sides by the wind.
Vidura too comforted the king, the lord whose eye was wisdom, sprinkling the Kaurava with water.
Slowly regaining consciousness and seeing the women, the king stood silent like one deranged, O lord of men.
Then, after brooding for a long time and sighing again and again, he reproached his own sons and thought highly of the Pandavas.
Steadying his mind again with fortitude, the king once more questioned the charioteer Sanjaya, Gavalgana's son.
Sanjaya, I have heard what you said. Charioteer, has Duryodhana not gone to Yama's abode? Tell me truly, Sanjaya, and repeat this account.

Thus addressed, the charioteer said to the king, O Janamejaya: "Vikartana's son is slain, O king, together with his sons, the great chariot-warriors, and his brothers, mighty archers, sons of charioteers who gave up their lives.
And Duhshasana too has been slain by the glorious Pandava, and Bhimasena drank his blood in rage in the battle."

My dear, my mind is overwhelmed by wrong-doing, and hearing that Vaikartana is slain, sorrow cuts into my vitals.
mahabharata:8:4.3	Among the Kurus and Srinjayas, those eager to cross over sorrow and foremost in weapons, who live and who are dead?
[Sanjaya said:] The invincible, mighty son of Shantanu was slain, O king, having killed ten crores of Pandava warriors in ten days.
Then mighty-bowed Drona, having slain throngs of Panchala chariots in battle, himself, the unassailable one of the golden chariot, was slain.
After Bhishma and the great-souled Drona had slain half of the Pandava army, Karna, son of Vikartana, was slain.
Vivimshati, O great king, the mighty prince, having killed hundreds of Anarta warriors, was himself slain in battle.
Then your son Vikarna, remembering the duty of a kshatriya, his horses and weapons spent, stood bravely facing the foe.
Remembering the dreadful afflictions many times inflicted by Duryodhana, and the vow he had made, he was struck down by Bhimasena.
He who held sway over ten countries led by Sindhu, who stood under your rule,
the very mighty Jayadratha, having conquered with sharp arrows eleven akshauhinis, was slain by Arjuna, O king.
So too Duryodhana's son, valiant and arrogant in battle, following his father's ways, was felled by the son of Subhadra.
Likewise Duhshasana's son, the heroic, strong-armed, fierce warrior, was sent to Yama's abode by Draupadi's son by his prowess.
The lord of the Kiratas, who dwelt by the sea and in watery regions, the righteous friend dear and honoured by the king of the gods,
King Bhagadatta, always devoted to kshatriya duty, was sent to Yama's abode by Dhananjaya through his prowess.
So too the renowned Saumadatti (Bhurishravas), heir of the Kurus, the brave king, was slain in battle by Satyaki, O king.
Shrutayus too, the Ambashtha, an archer among kshatriyas, fighting fearlessly in battle, was slain by Savyasachin.
Your son Duhshasana, ever skilled in weapons and arrogant in battle, was felled, O great king, by Bhimasena.
Sudakshina, whose elephant force numbered many thousands and was marvellous, was slain in the battle by Savyasachin.
The lord of the Kosalas, having slain many hundreds of foes, was sent by Saubhadra through his prowess to Yama's abode.
Your son Chitrasena, the great chariot-warrior, having fought Bhimasena many times, was felled by Bhimasena.
The heroic son of the king of the Madras, who increased his enemies' fear, bearing sword and shield, was felled by Saubhadra.
Vrishasena, of great splendour, equal to Karna in battle, swift with weapons and firm in resolve, in Karna's very sight,
was sent to Yama's abode by Dhananjaya through his prowess, remembering the slaying of Abhimanyu and his own vow.
Shrutayus, the king who was ever bound in enmity with the Pandavas, having proclaimed his hostility, was felled by Partha.
Shalya's valiant son, O revered one, Rukmaratha, brother and maternal cousin of Madri's sons, was slain in battle by Sahadeva.
King Bhagiratha, the aged, and Brihatkshatra the Kekaya, though valiant and exerting themselves, were slain by those stronger than they.
Bhagadatta's son, O king, wise and mighty, who ranged in battle like a hawk, was felled by Nakula.
Your grandfather Bahlika, together with the Bahlikas, was sent to Yama's abode by Bhimasena through his prowess.
Jayatsena, O king, the mighty son of Jarasandha, the Magadha, was slain in battle by the great-souled Saubhadra.
Your son Durmukha, O king, and the great chariot-warrior Duhsaha, who thought themselves heroes, were slain by Bhimasena with his mace.
Durmarshana, Durvishaha and the great chariot-warrior Durjaya, having done a deed not easy to do, went to the abode of Vaivasvata (Yama).
Your minister Vrishavarman and the charioteer of supreme valour were sent to Yama's abode by Bhimasena through his prowess.
The king of ten thousand elephants' strength, a great one of ten thousand elephants' strength, with his host, was slain by the Pandava Savyasachin.
The Vasatis, O great king, two thousand strong, striking warriors, and the valiant Shurasenas, were all felled in battle.
The Abhishahas in armour, striking fiercely, the Shibis noble in their chariots, together with the Kalingas, were slain.
Those reared always in Gokula, most skilled in battle, many thousands of companies, and the Samshaptaka bands, all of them, coming up against Partha, went to Yama's abode.
Your two brothers-in-law, the kings Vrisha and Achala, who strove mightily for your sake, were slain by Savyasachin.
The king of Shalva, a mighty archer, Ugrakarma by name and by deed, O great king, was felled by Bhimasena.
Oghavan, O great king, and Brihanta together in battle, valiant for the sake of their friend, went to Yama's abode.
So too Kshemadhurti, the foremost of chariot-warriors, O lord of men, was slain in battle by Bhimasena with his mace.
Likewise King Jalasandha, the mighty archer of great strength, having wrought great slaughter, was slain in battle by Satyaki.
Alayudha, lord of the rakshasas, Kharabandhu and Yanaga were sent to Yama's abode by Ghatotkacha through his prowess.
The sons of Radha, the sons of charioteers and their brothers, great chariot-warriors, and the Kekayas, all were slain by Savyasachin.
The Malavas, Madrakas, the fierce Dravidas, the Yaudheyas, Lalitthas, Kshudrakas and Ushinaras, O revered one,
the Mavellakas, Tundikeras, Savitriputras, Kanchalas, easterners, northerners, westerners and southerners, O revered one,
hosts of infantry were slain, tens of thousands of horses, throngs of chariots, and noble elephants.
Heroes with banners and weapons, adorned with armour and garments, who had been long and diligently reared in their families,
were slain in battle, O king, by Partha of unwearied deeds; and others of immeasurable strength, bent on slaying one another, also fell.
These and many other kings with their followers were slain in battle by thousands, O king—this is the answer to what you ask me. Such was the destruction in the encounter of Karna and Arjuna.
As Vritra was slain by Mahendra, Ravana by Rama, Mura felled in battle by Krishna, and as Kartavirya was slain by Bhargava Rama,
so that hero, with his kinsmen and relatives, arrogant in battle, having waged a great and dreadful battle renowned in the three worlds,
was slain by Arjuna in single combat, O king, with his ministers and relatives—Karna, the foremost of those who strike.
The hope of victory of Dhritarashtra's sons and the very front of their enmity was crossed by the Pandavas, O king, though you did not understand it before.
Though advised by your well-wishing kinsmen, O great king, this calamity, a great peril, has overtaken you.
You, O king, were thought to be wishing well to your sons who coveted the kingdom, but your acts were like ill-doing; the fruit of them has come to you.
[Dhritarashtra said:] You have told me, my dear, of my men slain in battle by the Pandavas; now tell me, Sanjaya, of the Pandava men slain by mine.
[Sanjaya said:] The Kuntis, valiant in battle, of great spirit and strength, with their kinsmen and ministers, were felled in battle by Bhishma.
Satyajit, equal to Kiritin (Arjuna) in battle in valour and strength, firm in truth, was slain in battle by Drona.
So too the aged kings Virata and Drupada, with their sons, valiant for the sake of their friends, were slain in battle by Drona.
He who was a mere boy, yet matched in battle with Savyasachin and Keshava, and unassailable even by Baladeva,
that Abhimanyu, having wrought great slaughter, skilled in war, was surrounded by six supreme chariot-warriors with their great ministers, and, as Bibhatsu could not come to him, he was felled.
Deprived of his chariot, that hero standing firm in kshatriya duty was slain in battle by Duhshasana's son, O great king.
Brihanta, the mighty archer, skilled in weapons and arrogant in battle, was sent to Yama's abode by Duhshasana through his prowess.
The kings Manimat and Dandadhara, arrogant in battle, valiant for the sake of their friend, were felled by Drona.
Amshumat, the Bhoja king, a great chariot-warrior, with his army, was sent to Yama's abode by Bharadvaja's son through his prowess.
Chitrayudha and Chitrayodhin, having wrought great slaughter, were slain in battle by Karna with wondrous manoeuvres.
The firm Kekaya-born, equal to Vrikodara in battle, was felled by his own brother, a Kekaya, through his prowess.
Janamejaya, mace in hand, the valiant son of Parvati's country, was felled, O great king, by your son Durmukha.
The two tiger-like men Rochamana, shining like two planets, were at once sent to heaven by Drona's arrows, O king.
And kings who fought back, valiant, O lord of men, having done a deed not easy to do, went to the abode of Vaivasvata.
Purujit and Kuntibhoja, maternal uncle of Savyasachin, were sent by Drona's arrows to the worlds won by battle.
Abhibhu, the king of Kashi, surrounded by many Kashis, was made to cast off his body in battle by the son of Vasudana.
Seeing the army roused again, King Suyodhana asked what befell the Kaurava at the time that had come upon the Pandavas.
Having unyoked their horses, hastening and afraid, they then reached a thick region and entered it, hiding themselves.
And likewise the Kaurava king, the great-minded son of Dharma (Yudhishthira), and Kripa and the others—what did those three do?
There those great-souled sons of the Kuru line stayed outside the city for a month, to complete their purification.
In this matter, O sinless one, many kinds of peace have been spoken of by you; what peace is there for oneself, even from many kinds of tranquillity?
Having crossed over, the king, his eyes brimming with tears, fell upon the bank of the Ganga like an elephant pierced by a hunter.
How was that king, whose ministers and sons were slain and whose support among men was gone, and the renowned Gandhari, when their sovereignty was lost?
The sun, O king, its disc covered with dust, rayless, was constantly seen at its rising with headless trunks around it.
[Vaishampayana said:] Having heard of the great destruction of the Vrishnis, the Kaurava king resolved on departure and spoke to Arjuna.
I wish to hear this; you are deemed all-knowing, permitted by the great sage Vyasa of wondrous deeds.
